THOUGHT: The patient has bilateral submucosal lesions localized to the torus tubarius on endoscopy and MRI. The diffusion-weighted MRI shows restricted diffusion in these foci and intraoperative biopsy produced draining purulence — findings most consistent with an infectious/suppurative process (abscess or infected cyst). Pathology showed benign respiratory mucosa with reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and mild chronic inflammation, which argues strongly against primary epithelial malignancy and supports chronic lymphoid/reactive disease of the nasopharynx (eg, tubal tonsil/adenoid tissue). Growth of Staphylococcus lugdunensis from cultures confirms a bacterial infection (this organism can cause locally aggressive soft-tissue infections). The absence of suspicious malignant histology, the purulence, and DWI restriction point toward infected nasopharyngeal cysts or tubal tonsillitis with abscess formation as the leading diagnosis. Differential alternatives that fit some elements of the presentation but are less likely include an infected Thornwaldt (nasopharyngeal bursa) cyst (usually midline), nasopharyngeal carcinoma or lymphoma (would usually show malignant/atypical cells on pathology), and other benign nasopharyngeal cysts.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Infected torus tubarius (tubal tonsil) mucous-retention cyst / tubarial abscess (bilateral) — most likely (location at torus tubarius, DWI restriction, intraoperative purulence, S. lugdunensis culture, benign/reactive histology).
2) Chronic tubal tonsillitis (ectopic adenoidal/tubal-tonsil hypertrophy) with superimposed bacterial infection/abscess formation — very likely (reactive lymphoid hyperplasia on pathology, chronic symptoms, focal purulence).
3) Infected Thornwaldt (nasopharyngeal bursa) cyst — possible but less likely (can become infected and produce midline purulence and DWI restriction, but classic location is midline posterior nasopharynx rather than bilateral torus tubarii).
4) Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (exophytic/necrotic tumor with secondary infection) — less likely given benign pathology and culture results, but should be considered if clinical course or repeat biopsy raises concern.
5) Nasopharyngeal lymphoma (or other lymphoproliferative disorder) presenting with lymphoid hyperplasia and secondary infection — least likely given pathology showing reactive (not atypical) lymphoid tissue, but included because lymphoid tumors can present in this area.
